title: A VLT/CRIRES+ study of helium 1.083$μ$m absorption features towards the inner Orion Nebula
summary: JWST NIRCam F115W observations towards the inner Orion Nebula revealed a diverse array of previously unknown dark features. The most likely cause was absorption or suppressed emission of the helium 1.083$μ$m triplet which lies in that filter. We have obtained VLT/CRIRES+ high-resolution spectrographic observations over a selection of different dark targets, confirming that the features are indeed explained by a reduction in the flux of the helium 1.083$μ$m triplet, a reduction that is fairly uniform across the line. The Orion Nebula is a blister HII region, with a dense, bright ionised layer on the far side from the observer near the Orion A molecular cloud and lower density gas elsewhere. Using a simple radiative transfer model, we show that dark features arise when emission from the dense layer is absorbed by intermediate density helium (e.g. in clumps, globules, or winds from objects like proplyds) on the near side of the dense layer.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRCam F115W imaging of the inner Orion Nebula revealed numerous unknown dark features; VLT/CRIRES+ spectroscopy confirms they are caused by spatially uniform suppression of the He I 1.083 μm triplet, which a simple radiative transfer model attributes to absorption by intermediate-density helium on the near side of the bright dense ionized layer.
AI.motivation: JWST NIRCam F115W observations of the inner Orion Nebula uncovered a diverse population of previously unknown dark features. The leading hypothesis was that these arise from absorption or suppressed emission of the He I 1.083 μm triplet within that filter, a hypothesis that required spectroscopic verification and a physical explanation.
AI.method: VLT/CRIRES+ high-resolution spectroscopy of a selection of the dark targets, confirming that the features correspond to a reduction in the He I 1.083 μm triplet flux that is fairly uniform across the line. A simple radiative transfer model was then applied to the blister HII region geometry of the Orion Nebula, with a dense bright ionized layer on the far side near the Orion A molecular cloud and lower density gas elsewhere.
AI.result: The dark features are confirmed to result from reduced He I 1.083 μm triplet emission/absorption, with the reduction being fairly uniform across the spectral line. The radiative transfer model shows that such features arise when emission from the dense ionized layer is absorbed by intermediate-density helium on the near side of that layer, e.g., in clumps, globules, or winds from objects such as proplyds.
AI.conclusion: The NIRCam dark features in the Orion Nebula are explained by absorption of the He I 1.083 μm triplet by intermediate-density foreground helium along the blister HII region geometry, identifying these features as tracers of clumps, globules, and proplyd winds on the near side of the dense ionized layer.

title: Slowly rotating white dwarfs in f (R, T ) = R + 2λT gravity: structure and stationary tidal response
summary: We calculate the structure and stationary tidal response of cold carbon fluid white dwarfs in $f(R,T)=R+2λT$ gravity through second order in uniform rotation. Equilibria are compared at fixed baryon number, with angular momentum also conserved during each aligned electric quadrupolar tidal perturbation. Negative coupling increases radii and dimensional tidal deformabilities over the common mass range. For the baryon sequence studied, background readjustment accounts for 95.8--97.5\% of the rotational enhancement at 40\% of each model's Kepler reference frequency. The explicit mixed rotational tidal contribution is positive and numerically resolved, but subdominant. At that spin, the enhancement relative to each coupling's static model decreases from 107.4\% in general relativity to 14.2\% at the most negative coupling, despite its larger absolute deformability. This reduction reflects less relative background expansion and a different Love-number variation.

AI.tldr: This paper computes the structure and stationary tidal response of cold carbon fluid white dwarfs in f(R,T)=R+2λT gravity to second order in uniform rotation, finding that negative coupling enlarges radii and tidal deformabilities and that background readjustment dominates the rotational tidal enhancement.
AI.motivation: The motivation, as reflected in the abstract, is to understand how the f(R,T)=R+2λT modification of gravity affects white dwarf structure and their rotational-tidal response, comparing equilibria at fixed baryon number and conserved angular momentum and dissecting the separate contributions to tidal deformability enhancement under rotation.
AI.method: The authors compute carbon fluid white dwarf equilibria in f(R,T)=R+2λT gravity to second order in uniform rotation, comparing equilibria at fixed baryon number and conserving angular momentum under each aligned electric quadrupolar tidal perturbation. The rotational enhancement is decomposed into background readjustment and an explicit mixed rotational tidal contribution, evaluated at 40% of each model's Kepler reference frequency, and compared against general relativity and across couplings.
AI.result: Negative coupling increases radii and dimensional tidal deformabilities over the common mass range. For the baryon sequence studied, background readjustment accounts for 95.8–97.5% of the rotational enhancement at 40% of the Kepler reference frequency, with the explicit mixed rotational tidal term positive but subdominant. At that spin, the enhancement relative to each coupling's static model falls from 107.4% in general relativity to 14.2% at the most negative coupling, despite its larger absolute deformability, owing to less relative background expansion and a different Love-number variation.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that in f(R,T)=R+2λT gravity, negative coupling enlarges white dwarf radii and tidal deformabilities, but the fractional rotational tidal enhancement shrinks as the coupling becomes more negative. This suppression arises because of reduced relative background expansion and an altered variation of the Love number rather than a smaller absolute deformability.

title: Double White Dwarfs with Circumbinary Disks: Evolution, Population Properties, and Gravitational Wave Signatures
summary:
Double white dwarfs (DWDs) are important multi-messenger sources and powerful probes of binary interaction physics. Close DWDs formed through isolated binary evolution are expected to have negligible eccentricities. However, recent observations have revealed that some eclipsing DWDs exhibit eccentricities of order $10^{-3}$ or larger. In this work, we investigate the interaction between a circumbinary disk (CBD) and the central DWD, where the CBD is assumed to form from a recent common-envelope (CE) ejection. Our models are the first to include CBD-DWD interaction in DWD population synthesis and to constrain disk parameters such as disk mass and lifetime. Our population models predict a correlation between the eccentricity distribution and the orbital period distribution of DWDs, which can be tested by future observations.
  Furthermore, we discuss the influence of CBD on the gravitational-wave (GW) signal. The CBD-DWD interaction can shrink the orbit and excite eccentricity, extending the time for which the system is individually resolvable by a future space-borne GW detector. Our results suggest that CBD interaction should be accounted for in population synthesis of Galactic DWD GW sources and the stochastic GW foreground.

AI.tldr: The paper incorporates circumbinary disk (CBD)–double white dwarf (DWD) interaction, formed from recent common-envelope ejection, into DWD population synthesis for the first time, constraining disk mass and lifetime and predicting an eccentricity–orbital period correlation and enhanced GW detectability.
AI.motivation: Isolated binary evolution predicts close DWDs should have negligible eccentricity, yet some eclipsing DWDs show eccentricities of ~1e-3 or larger. This tension motivates understanding a mechanism that can excite eccentricity, such as interaction with a residual circumbinary disk.
AI.method: The authors model the interaction between a CBD (assumed to form from a recent CE ejection) and the central DWD, and embed this CBD–DWD interaction into DWD population synthesis—a first—while constraining disk parameters such as disk mass and lifetime.
AI.result: The population models predict a correlation between the DWD eccentricity distribution and orbital period distribution. The CBD–DWD interaction shrinks the orbit and excites eccentricity, extending the time the system remains individually resolvable by a future space-borne GW detector.
AI.conclusion: CBD interaction should be included in population synthesis of Galactic DWD GW sources and the stochastic GW foreground, and the predicted eccentricity–period correlation offers a testable prediction for future observations.

title: Tracking the evolution of sub-Neptunes. I. Gyrochronology of planet hosting stars
comment: 17 pages, 5 figure, submitted to Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary:
Stellar age is fundamental for reconstructing planetary-system evolution but remains difficult to determine for unevolved main-sequence stars. Stellar rotation provides a sensitive age diagnostic and a temporal framework for investigating the evolution of close-in planets. This is the first paper in a series aimed at tracing the evolution of the sub-Neptune population through homogeneous ages of their host stars.
  We compiled rotation periods and stellar parameters for 4639 confirmed exoplanet hosts. Gyrochronological ages were inferred using a two-zone rotational evolution model and a Bayesian approach combining rotation periods, dereddened Gaia (BP-RP) colours, and literature stellar masses as Gaussian priors. Rotational tracks were extended to the terminal-age main sequence, beyond the empirical calibration range.
  We obtain gyrochronological constraints for 2204 host stars. Well-constrained ages have typical formal uncertainties of 10--15%, offering substantially greater precision than is generally achievable through isochrone fitting for unevolved stars. Inferred stellar masses agree with the literature priors, while model effective temperatures are consistent with independent determinations. Ages beyond the open-cluster calibration range remain model-dependent.
  The resulting homogeneous catalogue provides the age framework for investigating the evolution of sub-Neptune populations and the emergence of the radius valley. Stellar parameters, provenance, and gyrochronological results are publicly available through CDS.

AI.tldr: First paper in a series establishes homogeneous gyrochronological ages for exoplanet hosts to trace sub-Neptune evolution.
AI.motivation: Stellar age is fundamental to reconstructing planetary-system evolution but is hard to determine for unevolved main-sequence stars; rotation offers a sensitive age diagnostic and a temporal framework for studying close-in planet evolution.
AI.method: Compiled rotation periods and stellar parameters for 4639 confirmed exoplanet hosts. Gyrochronological ages inferred via a two-zone rotational evolution model with a Bayesian approach combining rotation periods, dereddened Gaia (BP-RP) colours, and literature masses as Gaussian priors; rotational tracks extended to the terminal-age main sequence beyond the empirical calibration range.
AI.result: Gyrochronological constraints obtained for 2204 host stars, with well-constrained ages showing typical formal uncertainties of 10-15%—substantially more precise than isochrone fitting for unevolved stars. Inferred masses agree with literature priors and model effective temperatures are consistent with independent determinations; ages beyond the open-cluster calibration range remain model-dependent.
AI.conclusion: The homogeneous catalogue provides an age framework for investigating sub-Neptune population evolution and the emergence of the radius valley; stellar parameters, provenance, and gyrochronological results are publicly available via CDS.

title: A JWST/NIRSpec Catalog of Low-Mass Candidates toward NGC 2024 from Multi-component Spectral Modeling
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Young low-mass objects in crowded, highly obscured star-forming regions are difficult to characterize. Deriving reliable physical parameters requires separating photospheric emission from complex extinction and circumstellar emission. We apply a multi-component spectral-modeling framework to JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectra toward NGC 2024, obtaining adopted fits for 78 sources. The framework incorporates atmospheric models, dust and ice opacities, and optional thermal emission. Most spectra favor additional large-H$_2$O-ice opacity over the baseline small-grain model, while a smaller subset requires additional gray opacity, potentially arising from large refractory grains. Some spectra also require a thermal component to reproduce the long-wavelength continuum. The parameters inferred with this framework, together with the NGC 2024 distance, yield radii and bolometric luminosities. Comparison with evolutionary models for young low-mass and substellar objects provides mass estimates and identifies 46 candidate members, 27 sources classified as background, and five uncertain sources. Candidate members show lower fitted surface gravities than likely background stars. Of the candidate members, 23 lie above the youngest available isochrones, plausibly reflecting the cluster's youth and uncertainties in model initial conditions. The resulting catalog provides a uniform characterization of the NGC 2024 sample and establishes a framework for treating complex extinction and circumstellar emission in JWST spectra of other obscured star-forming regions.

AI.tldr: Multi-component spectral modeling of JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectra of 78 NGC 2024 sources yields physical parameters, classifies 46 candidate members, 27 background stars and 5 uncertain sources.
AI.motivation: Young low-mass objects in crowded, highly obscured star-forming regions are hard to characterize: reliable physical parameters require disentangling photospheric emission from complex extinction and circumstellar emission.
AI.method: A multi-component spectral-modeling framework applied to JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectra, combining atmospheric models, dust and ice opacities, and optional thermal emission; derived radii and bolometric luminosities are compared with evolutionary models for young low-mass and substellar objects.
AI.result: Fits adopted for 78 sources; most favor extra large-H2O-ice opacity over a baseline small-grain model, a subset requires gray opacity (possible large refractory grains), and some need a thermal component. Classification: 46 candidate members, 27 background, 5 uncertain. Candidate members show lower fitted surface gravities than likely background stars; 23 candidates lie above the youngest isochrones.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a uniform characterization catalog of the NGC 2024 sample and establishes a transferable framework for treating complex extinction and circumstellar emission in JWST spectra of other obscured star-forming regions.

title: The upper main sequence in h and chi Persei
comment: 21 pages, 14 figures and 8 tables; Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics (October 25, 2026)
summary: Binary interactions play a crucial role in the evolution and eventual outcomes of massive stars. Rich young open clusters provide large coeval populations to constrain the effects of binary evolution. The Double Cluster, with a turn-off mass well above the threshold for core-collapse supernovae, is an excellent test bed for these processes. We used h and chi Persei, together with NGC 663, to constrain the evolutionary pathways of massive stars, particularly the role of binary interaction. We present spectroscopy of around 80 stars to obtain spectral types and derive stellar parameters. We combined this dataset with Gaia astrometry to evaluate their evolutionary status and possible evolutionary paths. We derived atmospheric parameters for almost 60 stars in the upper main sequence (B2V and earlier) and found broad agreement between two independent fully automated procedures. We identified the cluster turn-offs between B1 V and B1.5-2IV and differentiated this feature from the vicinity of theTAMS, where we found a population of B1-B1.5 giants, with a high fraction of Be stars. The bulk of the population in all of the massive clusters studied in the Perseus arm is consistent with single-star evolutionary models at a given age, but some B-type supergiants are much more luminous than any other cluster star. Their typical cluster kinematics and stellar parameters suggest a merger origin. Other lower-luminosity B-type supergiants seem consistent with the rest of the population. Kinematic analysis has indicated that most Be stars have not been dynamically perturbed by a supernova explosion. Those below the turn-off are likely to have been formed via case A mass transfer. The more massive Be stars above the turn-off do not display any other characteristic indicating a distinct evolutionary population (abridged)

AI.tldr: Spectroscopy of ~80 stars in the Double Cluster and NGC 663 constrains massive-star evolution; most of the population matches single-star models, while the brightest B supergiants and sub-turn-off Be stars likely arise from binary interaction (mergers and case A mass transfer, respectively).
AI.motivation: Massive-star evolution and final outcomes depend strongly on binary interaction, but constraining its effects requires large coeval populations. Rich young open clusters such as h and chi Persei (the Double Cluster), whose turn-off mass exceeds the core-collapse supernova threshold, plus NGC 663, provide suitable test beds.
AI.method: The authors obtained spectroscopy of about 80 stars to classify spectral types and derive atmospheric parameters, using two independent fully automated procedures. They combined these data with Gaia astrometry to assess evolutionary status and possible evolutionary pathways, and performed kinematic analysis.
AI.result: Atmospheric parameters were derived for nearly 60 upper-main-sequence stars (B2 V and earlier), with broad agreement between the two automated methods. The cluster turn-offs lie between B1 V and B1.5–2 IV, distinct from the TAMS region, where a population of B1–B1.5 giants with a high Be-star fraction is found. The bulk of the population in the Perseus-arm clusters is consistent with single-star evolutionary models at a given age. Some B-type supergiants are far more luminous than other cluster stars, with typical cluster kinematics and parameters suggesting a merger origin; lower-luminosity B supergiants match the rest of the population. Kinematics indicate most Be stars were not dynamically perturbed by a supernova; those below the turn-off likely formed via case A mass transfer, while more massive Be stars above the turn-off show no distinct evolutionary signature.
AI.conclusion: Massive-cluster populations are largely consistent with single-star evolution, but binary interaction is required to explain specific subpopulations: luminous B supergiants as merger products and sub-turn-off Be stars via case A mass transfer.

title: The light curve modeling of eclipsing cataclysmic variables: from period bouncers to nova-likes
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, to appear in the proceedings of the conference "The Golden Age of Cataclysmic Variables and Related Objects - VII" (GOLDEN2025), to be published by SISSA
summary: I describe the basic concepts used in developing the computer code CVlab V2.0, which simulates the light curves of close binary systems with accretion-disk structures. I provide a detailed description of the code, including its underlying assumptions, limitations, and applications, as well as prospects for future development.

AI.tldr: CVlab V2.0 is a software tool that simulates light curves of close binary systems containing accretion-disk structures; the paper documents its basic concepts, assumptions, limitations, applications, and future development prospects.
AI.motivation: Modeling the photometric variability of close binaries with accretion disks requires a dedicated simulation tool; the paper motivates the need to document and explain the design concepts behind such a code so users can correctly apply and extend it.
AI.method: The paper presents a conceptual and technical description of the CVlab V2.0 code, outlining the physical and numerical concepts underlying its synthesis of light curves for close binary systems with accretion-disk structures, along with its built-in assumptions and known limitations.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results; the outcome is a detailed reference description of the code, its assumptions, limitations, and range of applications.
AI.conclusion: CVlab V2.0 provides a documented framework for simulating light curves of close binaries with accretion disks, and the paper outlines directions for its future development.

title: A potential observational test to disentangle the companion of binary millisecond pulsar PSR J1928+1815
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. A&A in press
summary: Recently, the binary millisecond pulsar (MSP) PSR J1928+1815 (J1928) was reported to be experiencing regular radio eclipses. To produce the radio pulse emission and regular radio eclipses, this source was proposed to be most likely an MSP with a He star companion. However, the possibility that the companion is a white dwarf (WD) cannot be completely ruled out. Considering the uncertainty of interstellar dust extinction, it is difficult to confirm the nature of the companion star in the near-infrared and optical bands. Based on the measured mass function and orbital inclination angle inferred by the radio eclipses, the gravitational radiation can produce a period derivative of $-(6.8-9.6)\times10^{-13}~\rm s\,s^{-1}$ when the companion star of J1928 is an extremely massive WD ($1.4~M_\odot$). Therefore, its companion star can be identified as a He star with a mass higher than $1.4~M_\odot$ if the measured period derivative exceeds $-9.6\times10^{-13}~\rm s\,s^{-1}$. However, the expansion of a He star could cause a transfer of angular momentum from the orbital motion to the spin of the He star through a tidal interaction. The loss of orbital angular momentum results in a negative orbital period derivative, which produces an extra-contribution to the period derivative due to gravitational radiation. If the companion of J1928 is a $1.0-1.6~M_\odot$ He star, the predicted period derivative is in the range of $-(4.9-13.5)\times10^{-13}~\rm s\,s^{-1}$. In particular, the tidal interaction could help to confirm a He star with a mass of $1.35-1.5~M_\odot$. We also constrain the maximum evaporation efficiency of spin-down luminosity to be $0.006$ when the companion star of J1928 is a He star.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the spin-down (period derivative) signature of PSR J1928+1815, including gravitational radiation plus tidal angular-momentum transfer, to discriminate a He-star companion from an extremely massive white dwarf, yielding a predicted period derivative range of -(4.9–13.5)e-13 s/s for 1.0–1.6 Msun He stars and a maximum evaporation efficiency of 0.006.
AI.motivation: PSR J1928+1815 shows regular radio eclipses, which favor an MSP with a He-star companion, but a white-dwarf companion cannot be fully excluded. Interstellar dust extinction makes near-infrared/optical identification of the companion unreliable, so an independent, extinction-free diagnostic (the period derivative) is needed to settle the companion's nature.
AI.method: The authors use the measured mass function and the orbital inclination inferred from radio eclipses to compute the gravitational-radiation-driven period derivative. They compare this with the maximal contribution from an extremely massive (1.4 Msun) WD, and further model tidal angular-momentum transfer from the orbital motion to the He-star spin driven by He-star expansion, which adds a negative contribution to the period derivative.
AI.result: For a 1.4 Msun WD companion, gravitational radiation alone yields a period derivative of -(6.8–9.6)e-13 s/s; a measured value exceeding -9.6e-13 s/s therefore implies a He star more massive than 1.4 Msun. Including tidal interaction, a 1.0–1.6 Msun He star predicts -(4.9–13.5)e-13 s/s, with the tidal term particularly diagnostic for masses of 1.35–1.5 Msun. The maximum evaporation efficiency of spin-down luminosity is constrained to 0.006.
AI.conclusion: The period derivative provides an extinction-independent test of the companion's nature in J1928: values beyond the WD gravitational-wave limit point to a massive He star, and tidal interaction sharpens the mass inference. The companion is consistent with a He star, and the spin-down evaporation efficiency is bounded at <=0.006.

title: Current Sheets and Magnetic Reconnection statistics by Solar Orbiter at few to tens of Ion Inertial Lengths II: Conditions for Reconnection, and Current Sheet Planarity
comment: Revised version resubmitted to ApJ; 21 pages, 8 figures
summary: We present a statistical study of magnetic reconnection and current sheet (CS) properties at scales from the ion inertial length ($δ_i$), up to 86.4 $δ_i$. We analyze 103 hours of high-cadence (4 samples/s) in-situ Solar Orbiter ion data, collected from July 2020 to September 2022, which correspond mainly to slow and Alfvénic solar wind. We applied an automatic detection algorithm to find CSs of thicknesses near and above the ion inertial length ($δ_i$), and classify them as Alfvénic or reconnecting. The orientation of the CSs is consistent with an isotropic distribution of the discontinuities. The median ratio of reconnection jet velocity to theoretical outflow velocity is 0.71. We find that the diamagnetic drift reconnection suppression mechanism has no impact on the cataloged CSs, due to the symmetry of their upstream conditions. We find that a flow shear in the reconnection direction suppresses magnetic reconnection, and it is consistently greater for Alfvénic than for reconnecting CSs. Flow shear in the guide-field direction is too small to suppress magnetic reconnection in ion scale solar wind CSs.

AI.tldr: A statistical study of 103 hours of Solar Orbiter data identifies ion-scale current sheets in the solar wind and classifies them as Alfvénic or reconnecting, finding that flow shear along the reconnection direction suppresses reconnection while diamagnetic drift and guide-field shear do not.
AI.motivation: To characterize magnetic reconnection and current sheet properties at scales from the ion inertial length up to ~86 δ_i in the solar wind, and to test which mechanisms suppress reconnection at these ion scales.
AI.method: Analysis of 103 hours of high-cadence (4 samples/s) in-situ Solar Orbiter ion data (July 2020–September 2022), mostly slow and Alfvénic solar wind. An automatic detection algorithm identifies current sheets with thickness near or above δ_i and classifies them as Alfvénic or reconnecting. The study examines CS orientation distribution, reconnection jet velocity versus theoretical outflow, and suppression mechanisms (diamagnetic drift, flow shear along the reconnection direction, guide-field shear).
AI.result: CS orientations are consistent with an isotropic distribution of discontinuities. The median ratio of reconnection jet velocity to theoretical outflow velocity is 0.71. Diamagnetic drift reconnection suppression has no impact due to symmetric upstream conditions. Flow shear in the reconnection direction suppresses reconnection and is consistently larger for Alfvénic than reconnecting CSs. Guide-field-direction flow shear is too small to suppress reconnection.
AI.conclusion: At ion scales in the solar wind, reconnection efficiency is limited primarily by reconnection-direction flow shear, whereas diamagnetic drift suppression and guide-field shear are ineffective; this distinguishes Alfvénic from reconnecting current sheets.

title: An all-sky catalogue of Be transition stars from WISE and Gaia
summary: We present an all-sky catalogue of classical Be stars undergoing transitions between quiescent B-type and active Be-star phases, based on Gaia DR3 astrometry and multi-epoch mid-infrared photometry from WISE and NEOWISE-R. From a Gaia-selected parent sample of 4.2 million candidate OBA stars, we identify Be transition stars through correlated variability in $W_1$ magnitude and $W_1-W_2$ colour, which traces circumstellar disk formation and dissipation. The final catalogue contains 3,300 Be transition stars, including 2,743 newly identified objects, and provides a large, homogeneous sample for studying Be outburst activity across the sky. The median durations of the measured outburst and decay phases are 459 and 478 days, respectively, consistent with previous WISE-based measurements and compatible with the long disk-evolution timescales expected in the viscous decretion disk framework. As an initial application, we use TESS photometry for 3,017 targets to identify 63 eclipsing binary systems hosting Be transition stars, including 33 Algol-type, 17 Beta Lyrae-type, and 13 W Ursae Majoris-type systems. Among the multi-epoch LAMOST spectra, two sources show candidate radial-velocity shifts exceeding 20 km s $^{-1}$; their line-profile behaviour suggests that RV variability in active Be transition stars may be influenced by outburst-related line-profile changes rather than being an unambiguous indicator of binary motion. This catalogue provides a basis for future statistical studies of Be outbursts, disk evolution, and their connection with binarity and spectroscopic variability.

AI.tldr: An all-sky catalogue of 3,300 classical Be transition stars (2,743 new) identified via correlated WISE/NEOWISE-R mid-infrared variability, with measured outburst/decay timescales and a first application to binarity and spectroscopic variability.
AI.motivation: Be stars switch between quiescent B-type and active disk-bearing phases, but a large, homogeneous, all-sky sample of such transition objects is lacking, limiting statistical studies of outburst activity, disk evolution, and links to binarity.
AI.method: Starting from a Gaia DR3-selected parent sample of 4.2 million candidate OBA stars, Be transition stars are identified through correlated variability in WISE/NEOWISE-R W1 magnitude and W1-W2 colour, which traces circumstellar disk formation and dissipation. Outburst and decay durations are measured; TESS photometry for 3,017 targets is used to search for eclipsing binaries, and multi-epoch LAMOST spectra are examined for radial-velocity shifts.
AI.result: The catalogue contains 3,300 Be transition stars, of which 2,743 are newly identified. Median outburst and decay durations are 459 and 478 days, consistent with earlier WISE measurements and with viscous decretion disk expectations. TESS analysis yields 63 eclipsing binaries hosting Be transition stars (33 Algol, 17 Beta Lyrae, 13 W UMa). Two LAMOST sources show candidate RV shifts above 20 km/s, but their line-profile behaviour suggests outburst-related changes rather than clear binary motion.
AI.conclusion: The catalogue offers a large, homogeneous basis for future statistical studies of Be outbursts, disk evolution, and their connection with binarity and spectroscopic variability, while cautioning that RV variability in active Be transition stars is not a reliable binary indicator on its own.

title: Solar Ephemeral Regions Hales and Joys laws
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures. Accepted for publication in Solar Physics. Comments are welcome
summary: Besides the active regions and sunspots, the Sun produces many bipolar structures such as ephemeral regions,ERs, and even smaller magnetic bipoles. In this study, we investigate the smallest end of bipolar magnetic structures on the Sun, focusing on ERs using Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager full disk LOS magnetograms. We identify and track the emergence decay sequences of ERs to quantify their flux and morphological properties. Consistent with previous studies, we find that the flux distribution follows a log normal profile and the total unsigned flux emergence rate is estimated to be around 1.45 10^22 Mx/day. We find the ERs are almost uniformly distributed on the solar disc with a substantial fraction emerging outside the activity belts. A statistical analysis of ERs tilt angle reveals a weak adherence to Hales polarity law. The mixed signatures suggest that a majority of the ERs are associated with the large scale global dynamo, while the remainder most likely originate from the small scale dynamo. Overall, our findings indicate that even the small bipolar magnetic structures are statistically imprinted by the solar global dynamo. Our results bridge the scale between ERs and active regions, providing valuable constraints on how magnetic flux is structured and emerges across various spatial and temporal scales on the Sun.

AI.tldr: The paper statistically characterizes ephemeral regions (ERs), the smallest bipolar magnetic structures on the Sun, using SDO/HMI full-disk line-of-sight magnetograms, quantifying their flux, emergence rate, spatial distribution, and tilt-angle properties.
AI.motivation: Beyond active regions and sunspots, the Sun hosts many smaller bipolar structures such as ephemeral regions (ERs) and even smaller bipoles. The smallest end of this bipolar-structure spectrum is poorly constrained, yet understanding how magnetic flux is structured and emerges across scales is essential to link small-scale and large-scale solar magnetic phenomena.
AI.method: The authors use Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) full-disk line-of-sight magnetograms to identify and track the emergence–decay sequences of ERs, quantifying their flux and morphological properties. They perform statistical analysis of the flux distribution, total unsigned flux emergence rate, spatial (disc) distribution, and tilt angles, testing the latter against Hale's polarity law.
AI.result: The ER flux distribution follows a log-normal profile, and the total unsigned flux emergence rate is estimated at ~1.45×10^22 Mx/day. ERs are nearly uniformly distributed over the solar disc, with a substantial fraction emerging outside the activity belts. The tilt-angle statistics show only a weak adherence to Hale's polarity law, yielding mixed signatures.
AI.conclusion: The mixed signatures suggest that most ERs are associated with the large-scale global dynamo, while the remainder most likely originate from the small-scale dynamo. Even the smallest bipolar magnetic structures appear statistically imprinted by the solar global dynamo. These results bridge the scale between ERs and active regions, providing constraints on how magnetic flux is structured and emerges across spatial and temporal scales on the Sun.

title: The colors of protoplanetary disks - Impact of nonspherical dust particles on the polarized and total intensity colors
summary: Dust properties in protoplanetary disks remain poorly understood despite their central role in planet formation. Recent studies based on analyses of scattered-light images and phase functions provide promising insights into dust characterization, but the phase function alone is insufficient to constrain dust properties. Degeneracies between dust remain a major obstacle to linking observations to realistic dust models. We investigate the behavior of the disk color as a function of dust. We used MCFOST to generate synthetic scattered-light images from the visible to the near-infrared, in total and polarized intensity. We considered compact spherical grains using, irregular particles and compact and fractal aggregates using optical properties from the AggScatVIR database. Disk colors were measured from these images. For aggregates larger than the wavelength, monomer size influences color, whereas aggregate size has little effect, especially at low fractal dimensions. Polarized color is more sensitive to dust properties than total intensity color, because it combines the wavelength dependences of scattered intensity and polarization degree. Effective medium theory is reliable only for compact aggregates with small monomers, becoming inaccurate for highly porous aggregates or larger monomers. Effective albedo helps predict disk colors, but radiative transfer is needed to account for multiple scattering. For HD 100546, red optical-to-near-infrared colors exclude compact grains and organic-rich compositions but are consistent with amorphous-carbon aggregates, compact or fractal, containing large monomers. These results show that combining color measurements with polarized scattering phase functions offers a promising way to break degeneracies between dust models. Applying this approach to larger disk samples could better constrain dust properties and evolution.

AI.tldr: Disk color, especially polarized color, is a sensitive dust diagnostic that—combined with polarized scattering phase functions—can break degeneracies between dust models; for HD 100546, red optical-to-NIR colors are consistent with amorphous-carbon aggregates containing large monomers.
AI.motivation: Dust properties in protoplanetary disks are poorly constrained, and while scattered-light phase functions offer insight, they alone are insufficient; degeneracies between dust models remain a major obstacle to linking observations to realistic dust properties.
AI.method: Synthetic scattered-light images (visible to near-infrared, total and polarized intensity) were generated with MCFOST for compact spherical grains, irregular particles, and compact/fractal aggregates using optical properties from the AggScatVIR database; disk colors were then measured and compared against dust parameters.
AI.result: For aggregates larger than the wavelength, monomer size influences color while aggregate size has little effect (especially at low fractal dimension). Polarized color is more sensitive to dust properties than total-intensity color because it combines the wavelength dependences of scattered intensity and polarization degree. Effective medium theory is reliable only for compact aggregates with small monomers, becoming inaccurate for highly porous aggregates or large monomers. Effective albedo helps predict colors but radiative transfer is needed to capture multiple scattering. For HD 100546, red optical-to-NIR colors exclude compact grains and organic-rich compositions but are consistent with amorphous-carbon aggregates (compact or fractal) with large monomers.
AI.conclusion: Combining color measurements with polarized scattering phase functions is a promising route to break dust-model degeneracies; applying this approach to larger disk samples could better constrain dust properties and their evolution.

title: Small-Scale Magnetic Fields of Hyades M Dwarfs: Evolution with Age from the Pleiades to Field Stars
comment: Accepted for publication by The Astrophysical Journal (ApJ)
summary: Small-scale magnetic fields are derived for 18 M-dwarf stars in the Hyades open cluster through an analysis of Zeeman broadening in magnetically sensitive lines from the APOGEE spectra, resulting in mean magnetic fields ranging from 0.7 to 4.3 kG. Comparison with results for field stars hosting exoplanets and stars in the Pleiades open cluster from our previous works reveals distinct distributions of mean magnetic fields, reflecting differences in stellar age. Pleiades stars exhibit stronger fields ($2965\pm632$ G) and are predominantly in the saturated regime, while the roughly 500 million years older Hyades sample has weaker fields ($1925\pm1028$ G) with a larger dispersion, spanning both saturated and unsaturated regimes. Field stars show substantially weaker fields ($573\pm272$ G) and consistently occupy the unsaturated regime. Using the three samples, we derive the relationship between small-scale magnetic field strength and Rossby number, identifying saturation limits for the Rossby number ($\mathrm{Ro_{SAT}}=0.145$) and mean magnetic field ($\langle\mathrm{B}\rangle_{\rm SAT}=2452$ G). Within the Hyades sample, we find that, at a given age, cooler stars tend to have stronger magnetic fields. This trend is less apparent in the other samples, due to the broader age distribution of the field stars and magnetic saturation among the Pleiades stars. Comparisons with isochrones indicate positive correlations between mean magnetic field strength and both stellar radius inflation and photospheric spot coverage. We also find positive correlations between magnetic field strength and chromospheric and coronal activity, with stronger fields associated with larger H$α$ equivalent width excess and higher X-ray-to-bolometric luminosity ratios.

AI.tldr: Mean magnetic fields of 18 Hyades M-dwarfs (0.7–4.3 kG) are measured from APOGEE Zeeman broadening; combined with Pleiades and field stars, they yield a Rossby-number saturation law and link field strength to radius inflation, spots, and chromospheric/coronal activity.
AI.motivation: Small-scale magnetic fields govern M-dwarf activity, rotation braking, and radius inflation, yet their dependence on stellar age and rotation is poorly constrained. Comparing coeval clusters of different ages with dispersed field stars isolates the age/rotation dependence of dynamo-generated fields.
AI.method: Zeeman broadening analysis of magnetically sensitive lines in APOGEE spectra for 18 Hyades M-dwarfs; comparison with prior Pleiades and exoplanet-host field-star samples; fit of mean field strength versus Rossby number to derive saturation limits; correlation analysis with isochrone-based radius inflation, spot coverage, H-alpha equivalent-width excess, and L_X/L_bol.
AI.result: Hyades mean fields span 0.7–4.3 kG (mean 1925±1028 G); Pleiades are stronger (2965±632 G) and mostly saturated; field stars weaker (573±272 G) and unsaturated. Saturation thresholds: Ro_SAT=0.145 and <B>_SAT=2452 G. In the Hyades, cooler stars have stronger fields at fixed age. Field strength correlates positively with radius inflation, spot coverage, H-alpha excess, and X-ray-to-bolometric luminosity ratio.
AI.conclusion: Small-scale magnetic field strength declines with age/rotation period and saturates at low Rossby number, with a single saturation limit describing all three samples. Field strength is physically coupled to radius inflation, spot coverage, and chromospheric/coronal activity, supporting magnetically driven explanations for inflated M-dwarf radii.

title: Revealing the dusty shell of the semi-regular variable V CVn
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics on 21 October 2026
summary:
The semi-regular variable (SRV) star V CVn exhibits a highly variable optical linear polarization, yet its position angle (PA) has remained remarkably stable at approximately 100 +/- 20 deg. over several decades. We present a comprehensive multi-technique study of the system covering six pulsation cycles from 2020 to 2025. This campaign includes high-cadence photopolarimetry, spectropolarimetry, and the first interferometric observations of V CVn using the CHARA Array (MIRC-X and MYSTIC) in 2024 and 2025.
  Our photopolarimetric data reveal a significant increase in polarization, reaching peaks of up to 6% during the 2023-2025 cycles, while the characteristic anticorrelation with brightness and the stability of the PA persisted. The interferometric observations resolve the stellar photosphere but show no evidence of large-scale asymmetric structures, such as a bow shock or isolated scattering arcs, at the scales and sensitivities probed.
  Based on these results, we exclude previous models based on interstellar medium (ISM) interactions or static reflection clouds as the primary drivers of the observed polarization. Instead, we propose a circumstellar disk or flattened envelope, analogous to the L2 Puppis system, as the most plausible explanation. We hypothesize that this stable geometry may be shaped or maintained by the star's high proper motion, where ram pressure from the ISM interaction favors a flattened distribution of circumstellar material. Within this stable framework, the polarization peaks are interpreted as the result of stochastic dust clumps, likely triggered by the star's long secondary period (LSP), which causes episodic increases in mass loss. This combination of an ISM-influenced disk geometry and transient, LSP-driven dust clumps naturally accounts for both the decadal stability of the position angle and the highly variable polarization amplitude of V CVn.

AI.tldr: A multi-technique 2020–2025 campaign on the semi-regular variable V CVn finds polarization peaks up to 6% with a decades-stable position angle near 100 deg, rules out ISM-interaction and static reflection-cloud models, and proposes an ISM-shaped circumstellar disk with LSP-triggered stochastic dust clumps.
AI.motivation: V CVn shows strongly variable optical linear polarization while its position angle has stayed essentially constant (~100 ± 20 deg) for decades. Existing explanations—interstellar medium (ISM) interaction or static reflection clouds—cannot jointly explain a stable geometry and a highly variable polarization amplitude, so the physical origin of the scattering material needs clarification.
AI.method: Six pulsation cycles (2020–2025) were monitored with high-cadence photopolarimetry and spectropolarimetry, supplemented by the first interferometric observations of V CVn with the CHARA Array (MIRC-X and MYSTIC) in 2024 and 2025, resolving the stellar photosphere and testing for large-scale asymmetric structures.
AI.result: Polarization increased markedly, peaking near 6% during the 2023–2025 cycles, while the brightness–polarization anticorrelation and PA stability persisted. Interferometry resolved the photosphere but revealed no bow shock or isolated scattering arcs at the probed scales and sensitivities, excluding ISM-interaction and static reflection-cloud models as the primary polarization drivers.
AI.conclusion: A circumstellar disk or flattened envelope—analogous to L2 Puppis—is the most plausible explanation, with its geometry possibly shaped or maintained by ram pressure from the star's high proper motion through the ISM. Polarization peaks are attributed to stochastic dust clumps triggered by the long secondary period (LSP), which episodically enhances mass loss; this ISM-influenced disk plus transient LSP-driven clumps naturally reproduces both the decadal PA stability and the strongly variable polarization amplitude.

title: Evidence of flare and coronal mass ejection-driven shock acceleration of relativistic protons on 21 November 2024
summary: On 21 November 2024 at 17:55 UTC, a solar flare erupted from far-side active region (AR) 13892, with enhanced hard X-ray flux measured by Solar Orbiter (SO). It was associated with a coronal mass ejection (CME) travelling at 1436 km/s along the limb. This event produced a strong and widespread solar energetic particle (SEP) event at Earth, STEREO-A and SO, with proton energies exceeding 100 MeV. We investigate the relativistic particle acceleration during this event, focusing on separating flare- and shock-related contributions and linking spectral evolution to the CME-driven shock properties. We combine multi-spacecraft energetic-particle observations with velocity dispersion analysis (VDA), three-dimensional CME-driven shock reconstruction, and magnetic connectivity modelling. Radio observations and SEP composition provided independent diagnostics of shock- and flare-associated particle acceleration, respectively. VDA yields solar release times (SRTs) consistent with an early flare-accelerated particle population at all three observers, despite their broad range of helio-longitudes. At STEREO-A, the early release is followed immediately by magnetic connection to an efficient CME-driven shock. A 3D reconstruction of the type II radio burst location confirms a connection between Earth and an efficient shock-acceleration region several minutes later. Within the adopted models, the SO release precedes magnetic connection to the reconstructed front, disfavouring acceleration at the connected shock as the source of the earliest particles. Despite this diversity, STEREO-A and SO show similar spectral evolution, while the near-Earth spectrum extends to relativistic energies and exhibits a high-energy rollover. SEP abundances also show signatures of flare-related acceleration at all three observers. The analysis suggests multiple acceleration processes acting non-uniformly across observers.

AI.tldr: A far-side flare/CME on 21 Nov 2024 produced a widespread >100 MeV SEP event observed at Earth, STEREO-A and Solar Orbiter; combining VDA, 3D shock reconstruction and connectivity modelling shows early flare-accelerated particles at all observers followed by non-uniform shock contributions.
AI.motivation: To disentangle flare- versus shock-related relativistic particle acceleration in a widespread, high-energy SEP event and relate spectral evolution to CME-driven shock properties across multiple helio-longitudes.
AI.method: Multi-spacecraft energetic-particle observations combined with velocity dispersion analysis (VDA), three-dimensional CME-driven shock reconstruction, and magnetic connectivity modelling; radio observations and SEP composition used as independent diagnostics of shock- and flare-associated acceleration.
AI.result: VDA solar release times are consistent with an early flare-accelerated population at all three observers despite their broad helio-longitude range. At STEREO-A, early release is immediately followed by magnetic connection to an efficient CME-driven shock; 3D reconstruction of the type II burst location confirms Earth's connection to an efficient shock-acceleration region minutes later. SO's release precedes connection to the reconstructed front, disfavouring connected-shock acceleration for its earliest particles. STEREO-A and SO show similar spectral evolution, while the near-Earth spectrum extends to relativistic energies with a high-energy rollover; SEP abundances show flare-related signatures at all observers.
AI.conclusion: The event indicates multiple acceleration processes acting non-uniformly across observers, with an early flare-related component widespread in longitude and shock acceleration contributing efficiently only where magnetic connectivity is established.

title: SHAPE: Solar Heliospherical Analysis and Prediction of Eruptions A machine learning approach to solar flare forecasting
summary: Solar flares are the most energetic impulsive events in the solar system, and reliable operational forecasting of the rarest and most destructive M- and X-class events remains an open problem. We present Solar Heliospherical Analysis and Prediction of Eruptions (SHAPE), a two-phase deep-learning pipeline that bypasses sunspot proxies in favour of direct soft X-ray observations from the GOES X-ray Sensor (XRS). Phase 1 forecasts monthly flare counts, aggregated to annual totals, with a hybrid model: a cycle-shape curve anchored to published solar-cycle minima fixes the timing and mean profile, and a compact gated-recurrent-unit network with Monte Carlo dropout models the residual variability. Trained on the science-quality NOAA GOES Flare Report for 1995--2020 and validated on 2021--2025, it achieves a mean absolute error of 204 flares yr$^{-1}$, although it underestimates the 2024 solar maximum. Phase 2 forecasts the next day's strongest flare class (C, M or X) with a shared-trunk, dual-head LSTM operating on a 12-day rolling window of five intensity features, with an optional blend against an active-region physics score and a decision threshold tuned to favour recall of M-or-above (M+) events. On a 100-day chronological backtest, the classifier attains a true skill statistic of 0.351, a Heidke skill score of 0.335 for M+ events, a Brier skill score of 0.163 relative to climatology, and an expected calibration error of 0.023. A day-to-day persistence baseline is, however, competitive on both skill scores, showing that much short-term predictability in flare class is autocorrelation rather than learned structure. SHAPE shows that competitive flare forecasting is achievable with compact architectures that retain in minutes on standard hardware, without sunspot proxy inputs.

AI.tldr: SHAPE is a two-phase deep-learning pipeline for solar flare forecasting using direct GOES soft X-ray data (no sunspot proxies): Phase 1 predicts monthly/annual flare counts via a solar-cycle curve plus GRU residual model; Phase 2 predicts next-day strongest flare class via a dual-head LSTM, reaching TSS 0.351 and HSS 0.335 for M+ events, though a persistence baseline is competitive.
AI.motivation: Reliable operational forecasting of rare, destructive M- and X-class solar flares remains unsolved. Existing approaches often rely on sunspot proxies; the authors instead pursue direct soft X-ray observations with compact, fast-retraining architectures.
AI.method: Two-phase pipeline on GOES XRS data. Phase 1: hybrid count forecasting combining a solar-cycle shape curve anchored to published minima (fixing timing/mean profile) with a compact GRU network using Monte Carlo dropout for residual variability; trained on NOAA GOES Flare Report 1995–2020, validated 2021–2025. Phase 2: shared-trunk, dual-head LSTM on a 12-day rolling window of five intensity features, forecasting next-day strongest class (C/M/X), with optional blending against an active-region physics score and a recall-favoring decision threshold for M+ events.
AI.result: Phase 1 achieves MAE of 204 flares/yr but underestimates the 2024 maximum. Phase 2 over a 100-day chronological backtest yields TSS 0.351, HSS 0.335 for M+ events, Brier skill score 0.163 vs. climatology, and ECE 0.023. However, a day-to-day persistence baseline is competitive on both skill scores.
AI.conclusion: Competitive flare forecasting is achievable with compact architectures that retrain in minutes on standard hardware and require no sunspot proxy inputs. The competitiveness of persistence suggests much short-term flare-class predictability is autocorrelation rather than learned structure, motivating sharper baselines and evaluation in future work.

title: Solar Wind Turbulence Spectra and Correlation Scale from 4 to 50 $r_\odot$: STEREO and PUNCH Observations
summary: We investigate the radial evolution of solar wind turbulence using remote-sensing brightness observations from the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) and the first science-ready images from the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission. Exploiting the combined wide fields of view of STEREO's COR2 coronagraph (4-9 r_sun) and PUNCH's Wide Field Imager (WFI, 21-50 r_sun), we track the radial evolution of the power spectral density and correlation scale of density fluctuations from 4 to 50 r_sun. Line-of-sight integration systematically steepens the "usual" turbulence scaling laws by a constant offset of about -0.5 across all resolved scales, so that the energy-containing range (nominally k^-1) and the inertial range (nominally k^-5/3) appear as k^-1.5 and k^-2.1, respectively -- consistent with previous synthetic-image simulations. The correlation scale increases with heliocentric distance across the full range of heliodistances probed, in accordance with previous theoretical models and observations at closer distances from the Sun.

AI.tldr: Using STEREO/COR2 and PUNCH/WFI brightness observations, the radial evolution of solar wind density-fluctuation turbulence is tracked from 4 to 50 r_sun, showing line-of-sight integration steepens nominal spectral slopes by ~-0.5 and that the correlation scale grows with heliocentric distance.
AI.motivation: The radial evolution of solar wind turbulence over a wide heliocentric range is poorly constrained, and remote-sensing observations must be interpreted carefully because line-of-sight integration distorts intrinsic spectral properties.
AI.method: Combined remote-sensing brightness observations from STEREO's COR2 coronagraph (4-9 r_sun) and PUNCH's Wide Field Imager (21-50 r_sun) are used to measure the power spectral density and correlation scale of density fluctuations, tracking their radial evolution from 4 to 50 r_sun.
AI.result: Line-of-sight integration steepens the standard turbulence scaling laws by a constant offset of about -0.5 across all resolved scales, so the energy-containing range (nominally k^-1) and inertial range (nominally k^-5/3) appear as k^-1.5 and k^-2.1, consistent with prior synthetic-image simulations. The correlation scale increases with heliocentric distance over the full probed range, agreeing with theoretical models and closer-distance observations.
AI.conclusion: Combining STEREO and PUNCH provides a continuous 4-50 r_sun view of turbulence evolution; the observed spectral steepening is a line-of-sight artifact, while the growing correlation scale reflects genuine radial turbulence evolution consistent with theory.

title: Stellar wind variability in OB stars and its effect on mass-loss determinations
comment: Invited review for the MDPI Universe special issue "The Lifecycle of Massive Stars", edited by Jacco van Loon
summary: Virtually all stellar winds of OB stars exhibit variability in one spectral diagnostic or another. This review focuses primarily on UV spectroscopic signatures of this variability and on studies that have exploited it to reveal the presence of large-scale velocity and density structures in the winds. The review includes demonstrations that the physical structures responsible for the variations appear to be large, spatially coherent and rooted in the stellar photospheres. Furthermore, evidence is summarised that these structures can be optically thick to resonance line radiation and are dense enough to modulate the X-ray fluxes that originate in the wind. Also discussed, is how the structures can affect wind line formation and, as a result, the precision by which mass-loss rates can be determined. The potential of millimetre and radio continuum observations to constrain the radial stratification of wind clumping is highlighted, as a future path to reliable empirical determinations of massive star mass-loss rates.

AI.tldr: A review of UV spectroscopic signatures of variability in OB-star stellar winds, arguing that the responsible structures are large, spatially coherent, photospherically rooted, and optically thick enough to modulate X-rays and bias mass-loss diagnostics; mm/radio continuum is proposed to constrain the radial clumping stratification.
AI.motivation: Nearly all OB stellar winds show variability in some spectral diagnostic, yet the physical nature of the structures causing it—and their impact on derived wind properties—remains contested. The paper aims to consolidate the evidence that this variability traces genuine large-scale wind structure rather than incidental noise.
AI.method: Review synthesis of UV spectroscopic variability studies of OB winds, exploiting time-series and line-profile analyses to infer the geometry, coherence, and origin of the structures, and assessing their optical depth and density via resonance-line and X-ray diagnostics. It also evaluates wind line formation effects on mass-loss determinations and the prospects of millimetre/radio continuum observations.
AI.result: The variability is attributed to structures that are large, spatially coherent, and rooted in the stellar photospheres. These structures can be optically thick to resonance-line radiation and dense enough to modulate X-ray flux originating in the wind. They also perturb wind line formation, reducing the precision of mass-loss rates inferred from those lines.
AI.conclusion: Wind variability reflects real, photospherically anchored large-scale structure that materially affects spectroscopic mass-loss diagnostics. Millimetre and radio continuum observations are identified as the most promising route to mapping the radial stratification of clumping and thus to reliable empirical mass-loss rates for massive stars.

title: Episodic Protostellar Outflows: A Proper Motion Study in Serpens South
summary: Serpens South is a notable protostellar cluster with signatures of recent star formation, including a high protostellar fraction. Within the region, several protostars provide important mechanical feedback via outflows. We investigate the molecular outflow driven by the Class 0 protostar known as CARMA-7, which is located in the central hub of Serpens South. Two epochs of observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) with sub-arcsecond resolution capture the well-collimated, episodic outflow with distinct ejecta knots. This outflow, traced with 12CO J = 3-2 and SiO J = 8-7, appears to be mostly blueshifted to the south and redshifted to the north, with radial velocities up to at least 25 km/s. We present the first proper motion study of this outflow by comparing observations taken in 2017 and 2021. The measured proper motions trace the ejection history and refine the inferred outflow morphology. We find that proper motions of the 12CO J = 3-2 and SiO J = 8-7 knots range between 10 - 40 mas/yr, corresponding to 30-90 km/s. Using radial velocities and proper motions, we determined that the inclinations of the outflow lobes are ~60 -80 degrees relative to the line of sight. Finally, we measure ejection timescales as recent as ~10 to ~120 years, and we discuss this in the context of other known protostars with recent ejecta events.

AI.tldr: First proper motion study of the CARMA-7 protostellar outflow in Serpens South, comparing 2017 and 2021 ALMA epochs to characterize its kinematics, inclination, and ejection history.
AI.motivation: CARMA-7 is a Class 0 protostar in the central hub of Serpens South, an active protostellar cluster. Its outflow provides important mechanical feedback, but the outflow's kinematics and ejection history had not been probed via time-domain (proper motion) measurements, which are needed to refine morphology and constrain inclination and ejection timescales.
AI.method: Two epochs of sub-arcsecond ALMA observations (2017 and 2021) of the well-collimated, episodic outflow, traced in 12CO J=3-2 and SiO J=8-7. Comparison of the epochs yields proper motions of distinct ejecta knots; radial velocities and proper motions are combined to derive inclinations, and measured motions are used to infer ejection history and timescales.
AI.result: The outflow is mostly blueshifted to the south and redshifted to the north, with radial velocities up to at least 25 km/s. Proper motions of the 12CO and SiO knots range from 10-40 mas/yr, corresponding to 30-90 km/s. Combining radial velocities and proper motions gives outflow-lobe inclinations of ~60-80 degrees relative to the line of sight. Ejection timescales as recent as ~10 to ~120 years are measured.
AI.conclusion: Proper motions trace the ejection history and refine the inferred outflow morphology of CARMA-7. The measured inclinations and recent ejection timescales are discussed in the context of other known protostars with recent ejecta events, supporting episodic ejection in this Class 0 source.
